power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Over the last half century, we have made little progress in the treatment of schizophrenia.
A key contributor to this is an insufficient understanding of what is causing the disorder.
There are currently two 5 broad families of hypotheses: those focused on a dopaminergic dysfunction, and those focused on a glutamatergic dysfunction.

Based on recent findings that antipsychotic drugs exhibit cell-type specific and long-term effects on cortical circuit function, we 10 integrate the two hypotheses into what we call the control limit hypothesis of schizophrenia.

It builds on the assumption that schizophrenia is the result of a developmental miswiring of cortical circuits that is based on glutamatergic dysfunction and causes 15 aberrant cortical activity dynamics.
These cortical alterations likely underlie cognitive dysfunction, one of the core treatment-resistant symptoms of schizophrenia.
The control limit hypothesis further postulates that the brain responds to and can 20 partially mitigate these aberrant cortical dynamics by increasing dopamine levels in the striatum.
When this regulatory system is driven to a control limit and dopamine levels exceed a given threshold, psychosis emerges.
Beyond explaining much of the existing 25 data, the hypothesis makes several predictions about cortical function testable in mice and humans.
Schizophrenia is a frequently disabling mental disorder that affects about 1 in 100 people.
Despite over a century of research, the pathogenesis of the disorder is insufficiently understood.
What represents a particular challenge to etiopathogenetic theories of schizophrenia is the multitude of etiological factors along with a high variability in clinical manifestations of the disorder.
Evidence suggests a neurodevelopmental origin with (poly-)genetic and environmental influences acting early in brain development (Fatemi and Folsom, 2009; Lewis and Levitt, 2002).

text.text: However, to date there is no satisfactory explanation for why schizophrenia typically manifests with psychosis only in adolescence or early adulthood, following a prodromal phase marked by cognitive dysfunction and affective symptoms.
The course of the disorder is highly variable, but often follows a relapsing-remitting pattern, with life stress being an important trigger of psychotic episodes (Martland et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The course of the disorder is highly variable, but often follows a relapsing-remitting pattern, with life stress being an important trigger of psychotic episodes <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Martland et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: It remains unclear how the multitude of known etiological factors results in a pathophysiology that gives rise to the variety of clinical manifestations.
There are currently two prominent classes 50 of hypotheses for the pathophysiology of schizophrenia: the dopamine hypothesis and the glutamate hypothesis.
While both hypotheses are supported by ample empirical evidence, their integration into a unified account of schizophrenia remains challenging.

Here, we propose the 55 control limit hypothesis as a new way to integrate existing pathophysiological hypotheses in a coherent model that accounts for some of the hitherto unexplained manifestations of schizophrenia and offers novel, testable predictions.
Dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia.
The dopamine hypothesis postulates that schizophrenia is caused by a dysregulation of the dopaminergic system.

The central pillar of the hypothesis was the demonstration that dopamine receptor 2 (D2) affinity directly correlated with 65 clinical effectiveness of the antipsychotic drugs available at the time (Creese et al., 1976; Seeman et al., 1976).

text.text: It has evolved substantially over the years and now postulates that multiple problems interact to drive a dopamine dysregulation that leads to psychosis (Heinz, 2002; Heinz 70 and Schlagenhauf, 2010; Howes and Kapur, 2009; Kapur, 2003).

text.text: Glutamate (or synaptic) hypothesis of schizophrenia.
The second hypothesis focuses on glutamatergic circuit dysfunctions.
The glutamate hypothesis was initially based 75 on findings that dissociative drugs like phencyclidine (PCP) and ketamine can induce psychosis-like states in humans (Luby et al., 1962).
text.formatted: The glutamate hypothesis was initially based 75 on findings that dissociative drugs like phencyclidine (PCP) and ketamine can induce psychosis-like states in humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Luby et al., 1962)</ref>.

text.text: Because these drugs act on N-methyl-Daspartate (NMDA) receptors (Javitt and Zukin, 1991), the speculation arose that a glutamatergic dysregulation could 80 drive psychosis, possibly by triggering increases in dopamine levels.

text.text: The glutamate hypothesis thus postulates that dysregulated cortical circuits are a core circuit problem in schizophrenia.
This has since been supported by genetics pointing to risk genes in cortical and hippocampal neurons 85 (Singh et al., 2022; Trubetskoy et al., 2022).

text.text: In its most recent forms, the glutamate hypothesis proposes that a hippocampal and prefrontal cortex dysregulation affecting glutamatergic synapses leads to striatal dopamine increases and psychosis (Heinz et al., 2019; Howes and the late stage of the illness (Insel, 2010; Murray and Lewis, 1987; Weinberger, 1986).

text.text: At the clinical level, this notion is supported by the observation that cognitive difficulties, which are distinct from positive and negative symptoms (McCutcheon et al., 2023), are often apparent long before the onset of other symptoms (Brewer et al., 2005; Keefe et al., 2006; Reichenberg et al., 2006).

text.text: Cognitive symptoms are also present in the absence of antipsychotic medication (Fatouros-Bergman et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Cognitive symptoms are also present in the absence of antipsychotic medication <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Fatouros-Bergman et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Subjective cognitive and perceptual symptoms, so-called basic symptoms, are characteristic of the prodromal phase of schizophrenia (Huber and Gross, 1989; Schultze-Lutter, 2009).

text.text: Thus, cognitive difficulties are likely an integral aspect of the disorder.
This idea is also supported by findings of correlated anatomical changes in at-risk individuals with 110 cognitive disturbances and patients with schizophrenia (Koutsouleris et al., 2025).

text.text: Based on such considerations, it has long been speculated that schizophrenia is caused by a developmental miswiring of cortical circuits that initially manifests with cognitive symptoms and only later results in 115 psychosis (Schmitt et al., 2023).

text.text: Most antipsychotic drugs are thought to exert their effects primarily through antagonism at D₂ receptors (Creese et al., 1976; Seeman et al., 1976), particularly within mesolimbic pathways (Schmack et al., 120 2021), and, to some extent, through antagonism at 5-HT₂A serotonin receptors, which are prominently expressed on layer 5 (L5) cortical pyramidal neurons (Weber and Andrade, 2010).

text.text: However, it is still unclear how this D2 and 5-HT2A antagonism changes cortical circuit function in a 125 way that reduces psychosis.

Research in humans using noninvasive neuroimaging methods such as fMRI or EEG offers only limited access to cortical circuit mechanisms and cannot resolve cell-type specific effects of antipsychotics.
Accordingly, human neuroimaging work has not yielded a 130 clear picture with only small and highly variable effects (Debruille et al., 2013; Dominicus et al., 2023; Yoshimura et al., 2007).

text.text: However, using cell-type specific activity measurements in mouse cortex, a subset of clinically effective antipsychotic drugs was recently found to drive a selective decorrelation of the activity in L5 cortical neurons (Heindorf and Keller, 2024).

text.text: This effect is independent of the receptor binding profile of the drug and largely absent in neurons of superficial layers of cortex.
The decorrelation effect could be caused by drug-driven plasticity that increases long-range functional inhibition in cortex (Lupori et al., 2026).

text.text: Based on these findings, we have speculated that an increase in the long-range correlations between L5 neurons could result in false inferences that manifest as psychosis, and that the L5 decorrelation may be the treatment-relevant effect of antipsychotic drugs (Keller and Sterzer, 2024).

text.text: How an increase in L5 correlations may come about in the disorder, or how antipsychotic drugs lead to a decorrelation of deep cortical layers is still unclear.
Based on the considerations reviewed above, we here propose the control limit hypothesis, a novel hypothesis for the pathophysiology of schizophrenia.

It differs from the most recent versions of the glutamate hypothesis (Howes and Onwordi, 2023; Lisman et al., 2008) primarily in 155 proposing a mechanistic link for how cortical circuit miswiring results in increased dopamine levels: The dopaminergic system acts as a feedback control system to maintain cortical activity patterns within an optimal physiological range.

text.text: The first step in the cascade that eventually results in what we describe as schizophrenia is a developmental miswiring of cortical 165 circuits.
The primary disorder-relevant consequence of this neurodevelopmental miswiring is a specific functional shift within cortical L5 excitatory neurons.

Beyond a generalized excitation-inhibition imbalance typically attributed to synaptic loss, we speculate that a reduction in long-range 170 inhibitory influence disrupts communication within L5 networks, impairing their ability to transition fluidly between distinct network states.

Cognitive functioning relies on an optimal speed of these cortical dynamics, that is, the rate at which L5 ensembles transition between 175 stable attractor states corresponding to distinct representations.

If these dynamics become too slow, the network struggles to make appropriate associations, retrieve memories efficiently, or disengage from persistent representations, manifesting clinically as cognitive 180 dysfunction.
Conversely, a speed that is too high might result in thought racing, spurious associations, and false inferences, giving rise to psychotic experiences.
The speed of these cortical dynamics is likely tightly controlled through neuromodulatory feedback loops.

We postulate 185 that in the cortex, dopamine is one way by which the brain can control the speed of cortical dynamics, and that psychosis is the consequence of this feedback control reaching an upper limit.
According to the control limit hypothesis, the brain actively 190 counteracts abnormally slow cortical dynamics by increasing dopamine levels.
Dopamine modulates cortical activity through a synergy of direct dopaminergic signaling and indirect regulation via the cortico-striatal-thalamic loop (Figure 1).

text.text: Elevated dopamine levels accelerate state 195 transitions to keep cortical dynamics within a physiological range, thus potentially reflecting an allostatic adaptation.
If this control system is then additionally taxed by life stressors that further increase dopamine levels, the dopaminergic control of cortical activity can reach a control 200 limit.

High dopamine levels thus act analogously to a fever: an endogenous allostatic response to an underlying circuit problem (slowed attractor dynamics), rather than merely a pathological excess of dopamine.
When driven beyond a critical threshold, this response triggers severe side effects-in this case, an acceleration of cortical dynamics that underpins hallucinations and delusions.
Psychosis, according to this view, is the behavioral-phenomenological consequence of a regulatory feedback controller pushed past its operational limit.

text.text: It is thus unlikely that increased dopamine levels per se are the cause of cognitive dysfunction.
Rather, the brain may try to compensate for a circuit miswiring that underlies cognitive dysfunction by increasing dopamine levels.
According to the control limit hypothesis, antipsychotics downscale dopaminergic tone to decelerate cortical attractor dynamics.
On standard measurement timescales, this deceleration manifests empirically as a reduction in L5 network correlation.
While this slowing successfully reduces psychotic symptoms, it simultaneously exacerbates the underlying cognitive dysfunction.
Further findings that may be explained by the control limit hypothesis.
The control limit as a convergence point for multiple risk factors.

A dopaminergic control system that the brain uses to correct cortical activity patterns could also explain why the disorder is so polygenic with a very low penetrance of individual genetic mutations and exhibits a strong influence 340 of life experience.
Only when multiple problems coincide or amplify is the control system driven to its control limit, and the defining symptoms of the disorder manifest.
Many people have some of the genetic predispositions and experience life events that are risk factors for schizophrenia.
Yet, schizophrenia develops only in those in whom these issues coincide and the control system reaches its limit.
Explaining the clinical characteristics of antipsychotic action.
The control limit hypothesis may also explain key clinical observations regarding the effects of antipsychotic drugs.
If the brain uses dopamine levels to regulate the speed of cortical dynamics, this control is likely mediated, at least in part, by dopamine-dependent plasticity.

Dopamine is a well-established modulator of plasticity in 355 both cortical circuits (Huang et al., 2004; Kolomiets et al., 2009; Speranza et al., 2021) and cortico-striatal loops (Reynolds and Wickens, 2002).

text.text: Prolonged elevations in dopamine drive compensatory plasticity within these networks, structurally biasing them to faster dynamics.
Consequently, when antipsychotic drugs abruptly reduce the direct effects of dopamine, cortical function does not immediately normalize.

Because the cortical circuit has been sensitized by this extended, dopamine-driven plasticity, it must gradually undergo reverse remodeling, essentially unlearning these adaptations, before returning to baseline dynamics and providing relief from psychosis.
This functional remodeling would explain the relatively slow onset of action of antipsychotic drugs.
Furthermore, it accounts for why antipsychotic treatments become less effective the longer patients remain untreated (Marshall et al., 2005).

text.text: If chronic increases in dopamine levels trigger entrenched plasticity in how cortical circuits respond to changes in dopamine levels, this could explain why treatment is more effective when initiated early in the 375 course of the disorder.
Importantly, antipsychotic efficacy is not restricted to antidopaminergic mechanisms of action.

A subset of more recently developed antipsychotic drugs and candidate drugs in development do not target D2 receptors 380 or even the dopaminergic system in general (e.g., evenamide, a selective voltage-gated sodium channel blocker, or xanomeline, a muscarinic acetylcholine receptor agonist).

If dopamine functions as a regulator of cortical activity, and altered cortical activity is the neuronal 385 substrate of psychosis, there are likely other ways to alter cortical activity dynamics that do not involve dopamine.
Assuming the control limit hypothesis is correct, dopamine might just be an easy entry point, as it is the brain's endogenous way to regulate cortical activity.
Conversely, some patients are unresponsive to D2-blocking antipsychotic drugs.
The brain likely has other ways beyond dopamine to regulate cortical activity patterns.

The key novel assumption in the hypothesis we present here is that dopamine levels are used as a feedback control system to maintain cortical activity patterns within an optimal physiological range.
This hypothesis has a few directly testable predictions mainly related to the interplay between the dopaminergic system and cortical function.
Some of these can be tested using cell-type specific interventions in the mouse, others can be tested directly in humans.
• Increased levels of dopamine in the brain increase the speed of cortical dynamics.
We predict that experimentally increasing levels of dopamine should result in increased speed of cortical dynamics that can be measured as an increase in correlations in L5 of cortex.
• Long-term increases of dopamine levels drive aberrant plasticity of cortical circuits.

Long-term increases in dopamine levels should drive plasticity that biases cortical circuits towards faster dynamics, 455 and as a consequence increases in measured levels of cortico-cortical correlations.
• Genetic susceptibility for schizophrenia should manifest as alterations in cortical activity patterns.
We should find that a common feature of different genetic mouse models of schizophrenia is that they exhibit alterations to cortical activity patterns that bias them to increased correlations.
• Aberrant cortical activity can trigger increased levels of dopamine activity.
Dopamine release should be driven by a specific set of cortical activity patterns.
We predict that an artificial reduction in the dorsal cortexwide speed of L5 activity or L5 correlations results in increased dopamine release.
This can be tested experimentally by optogenetically inducing aberrant L5 activity patterns and measuring the resulting responses of subcortical dopaminergic neurons.
• Decorrelation of striatal activity by antipsychotic drugs.

As L5 cortical neurons are one of the dominant direct inputs to the striatum, and their projection preserves topography (Kemp and Powell, 1970; Lehéricy et al., 2004; Selemon and Goldman-Rakic, 1985), the decorrelation of L5 neurons observed after antipsychotic administration in mice should be 480 reflected in decorrelation of striatal activity in humans.

The treatment-relevant changes to cortical activity patterns should not depend on the molecular mechanism of action of the treatment.

Similar to the data in the mouse, we should find signatures of 495 antipsychotic efficacy in drug-driven changes to cortical activity patterns common to all treatments that are effective in improving psychosis.
• The influence of dopamine release on cortical activity patterns should be different in high-risk individuals.
In individuals at high clinical risk of psychosis, baseline dopamine levels are likely already increased.
However, it is not clear whether the cortical response to dopamine de-or hypersensitizes with prolonged increases in dopamine.
We would expect to find 505 characteristic differences in the cortical dopamine response of high-risk individuals.
If the dopaminergic system has feedback control over cortical dynamics, why does it fail to keep them within an 510 optimal range?
There are at least two possible reasons for this.
First, this could be the result of a mismatch between the anatomical resolution of the feedback control system and the anatomical extent of the underlying circuit problem.
For example, there could be a genetic problem in 515 part of the prefrontal circuit that results in activity dynamics that are too slow specifically in that part of prefrontal cortex.
Or the circuit dysfunction could preferentially affect lateral communication within only one specific cell type.

The dopaminergic feedback control does 520 not have the resolution to only increase the speed of activity dynamics in that part of prefrontal cortex or just that cell type, but can only influence all of prefrontal cortex (or all of cortex) at once.
Alternatively, it is possible that there is an imbalance of direct and indirect cortico-striatal 525 loops and dopamine acts on both D1 and D2 receptors.

As a result of such a resolution mismatch between the underlying circuit problem and the dopaminergic feedback controller, the system cannot fully compensate for the problem across the entire circuit at the same time.

Second, 530 it is possible that through an extended increase of dopamine levels, the cortical circuit or cortico-striatalthalamic loops are reshaped by plasticity to naturally tend to faster dynamics, making the network hypersensitive to even physiological changes in dopamine input.
Conceptually, this can be thought of as a dynamic decrease of the upper limit of the permissible dopamine range (Ashcroft et al., 1981).

text.text: We propose that the midbrain dopaminergic system acts as a sensor for aberrant cortical activity, specifically detecting changes in the speed of cortical dynamics, possibly by using measures of the correlation structure of deep-layer networks.
This sensing could occur through a combination of direct prefrontal projections and 545 indirect pathways mediated by the striatum.

Through these circuits, the midbrain dopaminergic system can monitor either a global increase in long-range L5 correlations or a specific decoupling in the synchrony between L5 intratelencephalic (IT) and extratelencephalic (ET) 550 populations.

When these patterns deviate from the physiological optimum, signaling a breakdown in efficient cortical dynamics, the midbrain dopaminergic system increases dopamine release in an attempt to restore circuit stability.
What is the role of cortical plasticity?
A secondary problem may be compensatory plasticity.
The efficacy of dopaminergic control is likely self-limiting.
We speculate that through a process of compensatory plasticity, the cortical circuit adapts to sustained dopaminergic signaling.
This would create a feedback loop that gradually erodes the intended regulatory effect, leading to a state of diminished responsiveness or tolerance.
Thus, to reach the same level of feedback control, the regulatory system is gradually driven toward its control limit.
Why is treatment onset so slow?

D2 receptor occupancy in the striatum reaches therapeutic levels within hours of initiating antipsychotic treatment, yet the reduction of positive symptoms typically develops over the course of days and weeks.
Why does clinical improvement lag behind 570 receptor blockade?
This clinical delay reflects the distinction between acute pharmacological blockade and circuit-level reverse remodeling.

While D2 antagonists acutely diminish the subcortical driving force on cortical dynamics, the cortical network has undergone prolonged, 575 dopamine-dependent synaptic plasticity (sensitization of L5 pyramidal ensembles and cortico-striatal synapses) (Huang et al., 2004; Reynolds and Wickens, 2002).

text.text: Consequently, the cortical circuit remains structurally biased toward hyper-correlated states.
Relief from psychosis requires an extended period of activitydependent "unlearning" to re-establish stable attractor landscapes.

This also explains why longer durations of untreated psychosis predict poorer long-term treatment response (Marshall et al., 2005):Prolonged duration allows maladaptive, dopamine-driven synaptic remodeling to become progressively more entrenched.

text.text: If dopamine elevation is considered a primary driver of psychosis, why does a substantial proportion of 590 patients fail to respond to D2-receptor antagonists and frequently exhibit normal striatal dopamine synthesis capacity?
Under the control limit hypothesis, the fundamental circuit correlate of psychosis is cortical attractor dynamics that are pathologically accelerated.
While we speculate that dopamine represents a primary endogenous controller of cortical attractor speed, it is unlikely to be the only one.
Parallel neuromodulatory loops, notably cholinergic and serotonergic feedback systems, similarly regulate L5 network dynamics.

In non-600 responders, psychosis may be driven by failure within one of these parallel control systems, which could explain why clozapine (a weak D2 antagonist with a profile characterized predominantly by 5-HT2A antagonism and partial agonism at muscarinic M4 receptors) remains uniquely effective in 605 treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
In addition, direct alterations to the L5 network itself can also accelerate attractor dynamics.
For instance, the psychosis observed in certain neurodegenerative disorders may be triggered directly by structural degeneration of L5 ensembles.
Furthermore, in longstanding or severe schizophrenia, chronic overactivation of the control system may induce profound structural remodeling within L5 microcircuits.

Once attractor barriers are structurally degraded, dynamic instability becomes entrenched and refractory to upstream 615 neuromodulatory tone; at that stage, simply dampening dopamine signaling can no longer restore attractor stability.
Overcoming treatment resistance will ultimately require novel biomarkers to stratify patients by the specific circuit mechanism underlying their symptoms.
What is the relationship between the cortical correlation structure and the speed of cortical dynamics?
We have used the phrase 'speed of cortical dynamics' as an intuitive shorthand for the underlying stability and depth of cortical attractor states.
When attractor wells become too shallow, 625 the energy barriers between distinct network representations are reduced.

As a result, the transition between attractors becomes abnormally rapid, or the network may even become bistable, allowing for the aberrant parallel activation of unrelated attractor states 630 (Loh et al., 2007; Musa et al., 2022).

text.text: These accelerated dynamics can drive an apparent increase in network correlation purely due to the temporal limits of our recording techniques.

Modalities such as calcium imaging and fMRI are restricted to timescales ranging from tens of 635 milliseconds to seconds, allowing us to measure broad correlation structures but not the true, underlying speed of fast attractor state transitions.

If dynamics accelerate, causing the cortex to rapidly cycle through, or simultaneously activate, distinct states within a single 640 measurement frame, sequentially activated neurons will appear to be active simultaneously.
Consequently, these rapid temporal transitions blur together over our slow measurement windows, manifesting as increased spatial correlation.
Measured hyper-correlation thus serves as a 645 time-averaged proxy for fast, shallow cortical dynamics.

Intriguingly, it is possible that the sensing of the speed of cortical dynamics by the dopaminergic system could also rely on slower biological integration mechanisms that are essentially sensing this resulting correlation structure.
Dopamine is thought to control the timing and vigor of cortically controlled movements through its influence on the striatum (Arber and Costa, 2022).

text.text: This concurrent modulation provides more drive to the target movement while reducing overall inhibition, facilitating transitions to subsequent movement states.

From a 665 dynamical systems perspective, activating D2 receptors can be thought of as decreasing the depth of attractor wells in the neuronal movement state space, allowing for more rapid transitions between actions (Puig et al., 2014).

text.text: When dopamine transmission is overactive, this state space becomes overly permissive, resulting in uncoordinated, involuntary movements (such as dyskinesias) because multiple motor programs are executed in parallel or in too quick succession.
The control limit hypothesis proposes that dopamine exerts this exact same influence via cortico-675 striatal loops on cortical activity patterns in general, extending beyond purely motor functions.
Excessive D2 activation results in cortical dynamics where attractor states are too shallow.
We further speculate that this mechanism explains why D2-receptor antagonist antipsychotics are highly effective in treating Tourette's syndrome.

If these overly shallow attractor states occur primarily in sensorimotor cortico-striatal loops, they manifest as involuntary motor tics; conversely, if they occur in associative loops, they result in the thought disorders characteristic of schizophrenia (McCutcheon et al., 2019).

text.text: The clinical divergence between Tourette's and schizophrenia may simply reflect which part of the cortex is primarily affected by the developmental circuit miswiring.
Would this theory mean that treating schizophrenia with 690 antipsychotic drugs is similar to treating influenza with antipyretic medicine?
If our theory is correct, antipsychotic drugs do indeed only treat the symptoms.
But like in the case of fever, this can be lifesaving and is the best treatment we have at the moment.

The control limit hypothesis of schizophrenia as proposed here provides a unification of the dopamine and glutamate hypotheses as well as a concrete circuit mechanism and experimentally testable predictions.
But what are the 700 implications for treatment and the development of novel therapies?
Our best hope is that research inspired by the control limit hypothesis will help us to find a way to drive targeted plasticity.

Effective biological treatment of schizophrenia will likely involve a combination of acutely 705 relieving the symptoms of psychosis with antipsychotic medication, followed by treatments that can drive targeted plasticity in the affected circuitry.

We speculate that in the short term, clinically the most relevant approaches to induce targeted plasticity will likely be electric or magnetic 710 stimulation that can be applied focally -e.g., repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS).

In the long term, we believe that it should be possible to develop small molecule-based drugs that take advantage of heterogeneous expression patterns of neuromodulatory 715 receptors, find a way to deliver such drugs in a targeted manner (e.g. via ultrasound uncaging (Ozdas et al., 2020)), or develop a gene therapy-based approach.

text.text: In any case, we believe effective biological treatment of schizophrenia will rely on a combination therapy that acutely reduces 720 psychosis and drives targeted plasticity to return cortex to healthy attractor dynamics.

Progress in understanding schizophrenia has long been framed by two major pathophysiological accounts: Dopamine (DA) Hypothesis: Classically views striatal hyperdopaminergia as the primary driver of psychosis.
Relation to CLH: The CLH reframes hyperdopaminergia not as the primary pathology, but as an allostatic compensatory mechanism.
The brain actively elevates dopamine to modulate the speed of cortical dynamics.
Psychosis emerges when this feedback controller reaches an upper control limit.
Relation to CLH: The CLH incorporates glutamatergic/interneuron miswiring as the developmental "first hit."

However, it extends this hypothesis by providing a concrete biological signal that triggers dopamine release (aberrant layer 5 correlation structures and slowed attractor dynamics) and explains why this cortical alteration initially manifests as cognitive impairment long before psychosis appears.

The computational framework of predictive processing posits that psychosis arises from an imbalance in the precision weighting assigned to prior beliefs relative to incoming sensory prediction errors (Adams et al., 2013; Corlett et al., 2019; Fletcher and Frith, 2009; Sterzer et al., 2018).
text.formatted: The computational framework of predictive processing posits that psychosis arises from an imbalance in the precision weighting assigned to prior beliefs relative to incoming sensory prediction errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adams et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Corlett et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Fletcher and Frith, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Sterzer et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The control limit hypothesis provides a physiological, circuit-level implementation for these computational phenomena by linking them to the stability and transition speeds of cortical attractor networks.

When the dopaminergic feedback controller exceeds its control limit, the resulting over-acceleration and destabilization of layer 5 (L5) attractor dynamics map directly onto key computational failure modes in predictive processing:

Priors collapse before sensory evaluation: If attractor states are excessively shallow and dynamic transitions occur too rapidly, internally generated priors may decay or shift before they can be effectively evaluated against incoming bottom-up sensory streams.

This yields an unstable internal generative model of the world that fails to constrain moment-to-moment perception, aligning with behavioral and computational findings of increased perceived environmental volatility in schizophrenia (Deserno et al., 2020; Fromm et al., 2023; Hauke et al., 2024).

text.text: In an attractor network undergoing rapid, erratic state fluctuations, baseline cortical activity is inherently non-stationary.

Minor sensory mismatches that would normally be filtered out as noise are instead registered as significant, highly salient unexpected events, translating computationally into an aberrantly high precision weighting of prediction errors (Adams et al., 2013; Corlett et al., 2016; Sterzer et al., 2018).

text.text: Rapid hypothesis cycling and secondary hyper-rigid priors: Unstable attractor landscapes can cause high-level networks to cycle rapidly through candidate hypotheses, which may manifest phenomenologically as thought racing.

Over time, to protect against this perpetual volatility, the system may adaptively develop hyper-rigid, unshakeable higher-order beliefs (delusions) as a compensatory mechanism to enforce stability on an otherwise chaotic lower-level sensory stream (Corlett et al., 2019; Griffin and Fletcher, 2017; Powers et al., 2025; Sterzer et al., 2018).

text.text: When attractor barriers become too low or cortical ensembles become hyper-correlated, the network can spontaneously settle into high-level attractor representations in the absence of corresponding bottom-up sensory evidence.

In predictive processing terms, this corresponds to top-down perceptual expectations completely overriding sensory reality, manifesting directly as hallucinations (Cassidy et al., 2018; Corlett et al., 2019; Horga et al., 2014; Powers et al., 2025 Powers et al., , 2017)).
